routes.description: Establish that people sometimes face genuinely available alternatives, exercise control over which alternative occurs, and thereby possess the kind of freedom capable of grounding responsibility.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by supporting alternatives and agent control, answering the inference from pervasive causal influence to exhaustive determination, and connecting that freedom to deliberation, normative requirements, and desert-sensitive responsibility.

motionBridge.description: Show that genuine alternatives and control sometimes exist and can justify responsibility for the action selected.

centralBridges.description: Explain why causal influence, probabilistic pressure, and reason-giving explanation need not eliminate every genuinely available alternative.
Supply a defensible basis for believing in freedom while addressing challenges to intuition, appearances, deliberation, and reason-responsive belief.
Show why responsibility and normative practices require feasible alternatives or desert beyond purely forward-looking behavioral management.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify the incompatibilist and possible compatibilist concepts at stake when control, fixed history, and the ability to do otherwise are compared.
Explain how reasons can make free action intelligible even if the final selection is not determined by a further cause.

routes.description: Establish that behavior remains within an integrated chain of biological and environmental causes, leaving no agent-controlled selection among genuinely available alternatives and no desert-based responsibility.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by connecting multi-timescale causal explanation to the exclusion of libertarian control, rebutting intuition-based and practical objections, and deriving responsibility practices that do not depend on retribution or earned moral entitlement.

motionBridge.description: Show that antecedent causation excludes genuine alternative control and therefore cannot justify desert-based responsibility.

centralBridges.description: Integrate immediate, neural, physiological, developmental, genetic, cultural, and historical causes into a continuous account of behavior.
Explain why expanding mechanistic evidence and the absence of causally independent action undermine reliance on experienced freedom.
Show how learning, intervention, deliberative inputs, and behavioral change can operate causally without agent-originating freedom.
Connect causal explanation to rejection of retribution and differential desert while preserving forward-looking social responses.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish agent control from randomness so that indeterminacy does not itself establish freely authored choice.
Account for gratitude and other responsibility-adjacent practices through evolutionary and mechanistic functions without presupposing free choice.

sections.title: Causal explanation, influence, and genuinely available alternatives
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the integrated biological and environmental causal account exhausts the explanation of conduct or merely influences choices while leaving some alternatives available.

sections.title: Intuition, scientific evidence, and the burden of proof
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether experienced freedom and intellectual appearances supply a rational default, or whether mechanistic discoveries and historical error require withholding or revising that belief.

sections.title: Control, deliberation, change, and reason-responsive agency
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether deliberation, advice, belief formation, learning, and reasons can constitute meaningful control or remain fully intelligible as determined causal processes.

sections.title: Responsibility, moral desert, punishment, and humane practice
sections.rationale: This issue connects the metaphysical dispute to the motion's responsibility clause by testing retribution, innocence, entitlement, blame, and forward-looking approaches to harmful behavior.

sections.title: Concepts of freedom, explanatory stopping points, and indeterminacy
sections.rationale: This issue clarifies incompatibilist and compatibilist definitions, whether choice can terminate explanation at an agent's reasons, and why randomness alone may fail to provide agency.
